image.alt: A drawing of a tall stone tower on an island, with a fire burning at the top.
image.caption: An artist's idea of the lighthouse at Pharos.

passage.p: Long before electric lights, sailors looked for fires burning on hills and towers to find their way into port. More than 2,200 years ago, the city of Alexandria in Egypt built a towering lighthouse on the island of PHAROS, just outside its harbor.

At night, a fire at the top warned ships away from dangerous rocks, reefs and sandbars. The tower was so famous that it was counted among the Seven WONDERS of the Ancient World. EARTHQUAKES damaged it over many centuries, and by the 1400s it lay in ruins. Its name lives on: the word for lighthouse is phare in French and faro in Italian and Spanish.

vakt.text: Stand up and turn slowly in a full circle, like the beam of a lighthouse sweeping across the sea.

passage.p: In 1822, the French scientist Augustin FRESNEL described a new kind of lens. Rings of glass PRISMS gather the light from a lamp and bend it into one strong beam, so a lighthouse can be seen much farther out to sea.
Every lighthouse along a coast flashes its own pattern of light, so sailors can tell one from another in the dark. By day, many towers are painted in stripes, bands or checks for the same reason.
